volumes.title: Keys and One Trunk
volumes.text:
I came to the Lamplit Goose on the third of October with one trunk, a headache, and my late aunt Berenice’s keys. The inn stands where the causeway leaves the marsh, two miles below Emberwick: the last roof before the reeds, or the first after them. I am Nell Garroway. Until last month I kept the books for a chandler. I have never drawn a pint.

My aunt left a letter on the bar. It gave the price of a bed, the name of the cook, and a warning about the goose. The last line was underlined. Light the lamp over the door at dusk, every dusk. Never mind the oil.

I lit it that first evening standing on a chair. It took four matches and a burnt thumb. But it lit. This is the house book, and I mean to keep it honestly.

volumes.title: The Goose Takes Charge
volumes.text:
November, and my second month as landlady of the Lamplit Goose, the marsh-end inn my aunt Berenice left me. I have now met the whole household. Mrs. Brewin cooks, and tells her saucepans more than she tells me. Old Corbin Slate keeps the stable and the fires. The yard belongs to a grey goose named Mrs. Alderman, who inspects every arrival and has so far approved of one tinker and nobody else.

Our first full table was six eel-catchers, wet to the knee. Mrs. Brewin gave them barley broth with leeks, then a bacon pudding, and I carried the plates. I can now manage three. The fourth went into a lap.

The eel-catcher laughed and ate it from there. At dusk I lit the lamp over the door with two matches. Corbin said my aunt used one, but he said it kindly.

volumes.title: How the House Was Named
volumes.text:
December at the Lamplit Goose. Snow lay on the causeway and nobody came, so Corbin Slate, our ostler, told me how the inn got its name. I am the new landlady, and it seemed a thing I ought to know.

The first landlord, he says, was a marshman called Jeb Tolliver, who went out after stray sheep and lost himself in a fog a yard thick. He stood still, as marshmen are taught. Then he heard his own goose, shouting from his own doorstep, and he walked home along the noise. Next morning he hung a lantern over the door, so that nobody after him would need a goose.

It is a good story. I went to trim the lamp and found the oil can in the porch brim full. I have not filled it once. I supposed Mrs. Brewin had, and thought no more of it.

volumes.title: Fog on the Causeway
volumes.text:
January. I have kept the Lamplit Goose, on the marsh causeway, for three months, and last night the house earned its sign. A fog came up off the marsh at four. By six I could not see the pump from the kitchen door. I lit the lamp over the porch and turned the wick up high.

At nine the Grey Coast coach walked in out of nothing, the driver leading his horses by hand. He had steered by our light for the last mile. Seven passengers: a piano tuner, a draper, twin sisters with a parrot, and a family of three. We have five beds. The twins took the settle and the parrot took the mantelpiece.

Mrs. Brewin made one pan of onion soup go round eleven people. This morning I thanked her for keeping the lamp can filled. She said she had never touched it.

volumes.title: The Oil Question
volumes.text:
February, a slow month at the Lamplit Goose, and I spent three evenings with my late aunt’s account books. I was a bookkeeper before I was a landlady. A full oil can that nobody fills is an entry without a receipt, and I cannot leave it alone.

Aunt Berenice bought candles, lamp wick, soap, and an alarming quantity of mustard. In twenty-two years of ledgers she did not buy one pint of lamp oil. Yet the lamp over our door has burned every night, and the can in the porch is full this minute.

I asked Corbin Slate, our ostler. He scratched his chin. It had always been full, he said. He had supposed my aunt saw to it. Her letter to me says only: never mind the oil. I mind it a good deal. Mrs. Alderman, the yard goose, knows something, but she is not saying.

volumes.title: A Watch Kept Badly
volumes.text:
March. Somebody fills the oil can in the porch of the Lamplit Goose, and it is not me, the cook, or the ostler. Being landlady, I decided to find out, and on Wednesday night I sat up in the porch with two blankets and a flask of tea.

Mrs. Alderman, our yard goose, sat up with me, which I took for loyalty. At midnight the can was a third full. I checked at one and at two. After that I remember the goose settling against my boots, very warm.

I woke at six with a stiff neck. The can was full. There was a smell of horse liniment on the handle, and in the frost by the step lay two wheel marks, already softening. The goose had not made a sound. She shouts at curates and bank clerks, but whoever came, she knew them. It was Thursday morning.

volumes.title: The Painter Pays in Paint
volumes.text:
April at the Lamplit Goose, the inn I keep at the edge of the marsh. A travelling painter, Mr. Lysander Voke, stayed nine nights and discovered on the tenth that he had no money. He offered to repaint our sign instead. I have been landlady six months and know a bad bargain. This was not one.

The old goose on the board had faded to a pudding. Mr. Voke gave her white feathers, an orange beak, and a brass lantern with a yellow flame in it. Mrs. Alderman, our real goose, stood under the ladder and seemed to think it a fair likeness.

He told me one thing more. Up the ladder early on Thursday, he had seen a cart stop at our porch and go on towards the coast. He took it for a delivery. So do I, now. But nobody here has ever been sent a bill.

volumes.title: The Marshmen’s Dinner
volumes.text:
May, and the Lamplit Goose held the Marshmen’s Dinner, as it does every spring. Forty reed-cutters and eel-catchers sat down in a room that holds thirty. I am the landlady, and it was my first.

Mrs. Brewin sent out pea soup, a great raised pork pie, new potatoes with mint, and a gooseberry fool. My part was the bread. I forgot it. Forty men looked politely at their soup until an old reed-cutter stood up and said that Berenice, my aunt, forgot the bread in her first year too, and the mustard in her second.

They cheered. I fetched the loaves and was made to sit at the top of the table. Afterwards, with the yard full of lanterns and singing, I went out and lit our own lamp over the door. One match. I looked round for someone to tell, and there was only the goose.

volumes.title: The Night It Went Out
volumes.text:
June. The nights are so short on the marsh that the lamp over the door of the Lamplit Goose hardly seems worth a match. I am the landlady, and I will set down plainly that on the twentieth, tired after a wedding party, I went to bed without lighting it. It was the first dark night that door has had in anyone’s memory.

At eleven there was a knocking. On the step stood Bram Tully, the Emberwick carrier, a broad, slow man of sixty who has never taken more than a mug of tea in this house. He had his hat in both hands. “Your lamp’s out, missus,” he said. “I thought you might be ill.”

I lit it while he watched. He nodded and went back to his cart. I stood wondering why a carrier should look so shaken over one small flame.

volumes.title: Counting Thursdays
volumes.text:
July at the Lamplit Goose, where I am landlady and, lately, a spy. Somebody has kept the lamp can in our porch filled for years without sending a bill. For four weeks I have dipped that can every morning with a marked stick.

The figures are plain. The oil goes down a little each night. It is lowest on Wednesday. On Thursday morning it is full. Bram Tully, the carrier, passes our door before dawn on Thursdays, bound for the Grey Coast. He rubs his old mare’s knees with liniment; I have smelled it on him in the yard, and once on the handle of the can. And he alone, of all the road, came knocking in June when the lamp was dark.

So I know who. A ledger would stop there. I find I want the reason, and that is not in any column.

volumes.title: What the Carrier Said
volumes.text:
August. On Thursday I got up at four, made tea, and waited in the porch of the Lamplit Goose, the marsh inn I keep. At five a cart stopped. Bram Tully, the carrier, climbed down with a stone jar of lamp oil and found the landlady holding out a mug.

He took it and told me. Fifty-one years ago he was nine, riding the causeway with his father, when the fog came down and a wheel went off the edge. His father could not leave the horse. He sent the boy ahead, towards one yellow light. It was this lamp. Men went back with ropes. A quart of oil a week had seemed little enough.

My aunt never mentioned it, he said. But there was a bun on the porch shelf of a Thursday. He asked me not to make anything of it. I said I would not.

volumes.title: A Year of Lamplight
volumes.text:
October again. A year ago I came to the Lamplit Goose with one trunk and my aunt Berenice’s keys, and could not draw a pint. I can now carry four plates. Mrs. Brewin has begun telling me things before she tells her saucepans, and Mrs. Alderman, the goose, let a commercial traveller cross the yard unchallenged. Corbin says that is a sign of settled times.

Today I turned to the front of the house book, where the landlords have signed since Jeb Tolliver made his mark. Under Berenice Garroway I wrote Nell Garroway, and blotted it.

The first fog came in at five. I lit the lamp with one match. It is Wednesday, so before bed I put a currant bun on the porch shelf, under a basin, out of the goose’s reach. The can will be full in the morning. I shall not be minding the oil.

volumes.title: In by Ten
volumes.text:
Rule One. Lodgers shall be in by ten o’clock, when the door will be locked.

Mr. Aldous Pym painted this on a board the week he inherited the Three Kettles, on Cooper’s Row in Emberwick. His uncle Barnaby had kept the house for forty years without a single rule. There were four lodgers, who had come with the building like the damp: a piano tuner, a retired barge captain, a widow, and a young clerk in the attic. Aldous had been a clerk himself, at a ribbon warehouse, and he believed in notices.

At ten he locked the front door. At five past he remembered that he was standing on the outside of it, having stepped into the street to see whether the board hung straight. It did. He was admitted through the scullery window by Miss Thessaly Brandt, the piano tuner, who held the sash and said nothing.

volumes.title: The Midnight Cheese
volumes.text:
Rule Two. No cooking shall be done in the rooms.

The Three Kettles had a kitchen, and its landlord, Mr. Aldous Pym, felt that food should stay in it. The rule was aimed at the second floor back, where Mrs. Odalys Crumb, a widow of cheerful habits, toasted cheese at midnight. On the first night the smell came down the stairs. Mr. Pym went up in his dressing gown with a candle and a prepared remark.

Mrs. Crumb opened the door holding a long fork. She explained her method while he waited to speak: thick bread, hard cheese grated fine, a little mustard, a splash of ale, and patience. He came down forty minutes later, having eaten two slices and delivered none of the remark. Next morning he added three words to the board in smaller paint: after eleven o’clock. Even he was not sure what this meant.

volumes.title: The Hen Signs In
volumes.text:
Rule Three. No livestock shall be kept above the ground floor.

Mr. Aldous Pym, landlord of the Three Kettles in Emberwick, wrote this after meeting a speckled hen on the second landing. She was called Marigold. She belonged to Mrs. Crumb, the widow in the back room, and had lived upstairs for six years, coming down each morning to lay one egg in the umbrella stand. Mr. Pym pointed to the board.

The four lodgers gathered in the hall. Captain Fenn, the retired bargeman, observed that the rule said kept. Nobody kept Marigold. She came and went. Miss Brandt, the piano tuner, fetched the visitors’ book from the bar. The entry may still be seen, in Mrs. Crumb’s round hand: Marigold, of this town, one night, renewed daily. Payment, one egg. Mr. Pym had his boiled, and found he could not complain of a guest who settled so promptly.

volumes.title: Between Four and Six
volumes.text:
Rule Four. Musical practice shall be confined to the hours between four and six.

There was a bassoon in the attic of the Three Kettles. It belonged to Mr. Tobias Wren, a clerk at the corn exchange, who had been learning one tune for eleven months. The landlord, Mr. Aldous Pym, had heard that tune at breakfast, at midnight, and once during a thunderstorm. The lodgers obeyed his rule to the minute.

At four the bassoon began. At four also Miss Brandt, the piano tuner, sat down to the parlour upright with her tuning fork; and Captain Fenn, shaving for the evening, sang a barge song in a key of his own. By half past a small crowd had gathered on Cooper’s Row, and a boy was selling them apples. Mr. Pym stood with his fingers in his ears and reflected that the noise had not been reduced, only collected.

volumes.title: Beans at the Window
volumes.text:
Rule Five. Nothing shall be grown from the windows of this house.

Captain Orlo Fenn had worked barges on the river Ember for forty years and retired to the first floor back of the Three Kettles, where he missed having something to tend. So he grew runner beans. They started in a tub in the yard, went up the drainpipe, and by August were looking in at every window. The landlord, Mr. Aldous Pym, woke to find a tendril wound twice round his curtain rod, and painted Rule Five before breakfast.

The Captain read it and pointed out that the beans grew from the yard. They arrived at the windows. That evening a dish came to Mr. Pym’s table: beans sliced thin, boiled, with butter and pepper. He ate them all. The scarlet flowers stayed at his window until the frost, and he was seen, once, watering the tub.

volumes.title: Rent in Coin
volumes.text:
Rule Six. Rent is due on the first of the month, in coin.

Mr. Aldous Pym had kept the Three Kettles for half a year when he sat down with his late uncle’s rent book and found no money in it at all. Uncle Barnaby had taken payment in kind. Miss Brandt tuned the pianos. Captain Fenn mended the roof, the pump, and the back gate. Mrs. Crumb supplied eggs and the Sunday pudding. Young Mr. Wren, in the attic, did the accounts.

Aldous had been a clerk. He priced it all fairly, in two columns, and added it twice. By his reckoning the house owed its lodgers eleven shillings a month. He looked at the board for some time. Then he took a small brush and wrote beneath Rule Six, or its honest equivalent, and went up to ask Mr. Wren, rather humbly, whether the accounts might continue.

volumes.title: The Parlour Moves Back
volumes.text:
Rule Seven. Lodgers shall not rearrange the furniture of the public rooms.

In February Mr. Aldous Pym, landlord of the Three Kettles, spent a week in bed with a cold. His four lodgers ran the house. Mrs. Crumb cooked, Captain Fenn kept the bar, and Miss Brandt carried up broth and the news. When he came down, the parlour had changed. The settle was by the fire. The round table stood in the window. The piano had turned its back to the draught.

It was, Miss Brandt mentioned, how his uncle Barnaby had it, and Aldous had to admit that the room looked, for once, as if people sat in it. He wrote the rule anyway, on principle, and moved nothing. That morning a letter lay on the hall table. A Mr. Hobart Sleek, grain merchant, wished to buy the building for a warehouse, and named a handsome price.

volumes.title: A Letter Left Lying
volumes.text:
Rule Eight. Lodgers shall not read the landlord’s correspondence.

The letter lay on the hall table of the Three Kettles for a morning before Mr. Aldous Pym, the landlord, put it in his pocket. It was from Mr. Hobart Sleek, a grain merchant, offering to buy the house for a warehouse. Aldous had come to innkeeping from a ribbon warehouse, with no great love for it, and the price was handsome. He painted Rule Eight that afternoon, which was rather late.

Nobody admitted to reading anything. But that week Mrs. Crumb’s Sunday pudding came out flat. Captain Fenn left a slate loose on the roof. Mr. Wren’s bassoon was silent, and Miss Brandt, tuning the parlour piano, played only the slow pieces. Even Marigold the hen laid her egg in the coal scuttle instead of the umbrella stand. Aldous found it there, and stood holding it, feeling unreasonably accused.

volumes.title: The Perfect Lodgers
volumes.text:
Rule Nine. No lodger shall address a prospective purchaser.

Mr. Hobart Sleek, grain merchant, came to view the Three Kettles on a Tuesday. The landlord, Mr. Aldous Pym, had dreaded what his four lodgers might say to the man. They said nothing. They kept Rule Nine, and for that one day every other rule on the board as well. No bassoon sounded. No cheese was toasted. The hen stayed in the yard, and at ten that night four doors closed quietly. The house was as silent as a cupboard.

Mr. Sleek was delighted. A tidy, empty sort of place, he said; no trouble to clear. He would send the papers. Aldous saw him out and came back into a hall that smelled of nothing. He had spent most of a year asking for exactly this. He sat down on the stairs and did not like it at all.

volumes.title: Supper on Sundays
volumes.text:
Rule Ten. The landlord shall take his supper with the house on Sundays.

Mr. Aldous Pym did not write this rule. He found it on the board of the Three Kettles one Sunday morning, in white chalk, in four different hands. He was the landlord, and halfway through selling the building to a grain merchant, and he had not expected orders from his lodgers. He went, however.

The round table in the parlour was laid for five. Mrs. Crumb had made toasted cheese and a pudding. Captain Fenn brought a jar of his runner beans, salted in autumn. There were six boiled eggs from Marigold the hen, and afterwards Miss Brandt played while Mr. Wren got through his bassoon tune without stopping. Nobody mentioned the sale. Captain Fenn remarked that a barge could be sold, but not its crew. Aldous took more pudding and went to bed very thoughtful.

volumes.title: A Vote of the House
volumes.text:
Rule Eleven. No rule shall be added to this board without a vote of the house.

Mr. Aldous Pym painted this one in good black paint, the morning after he wrote to Mr. Hobart Sleek. His letter was short. The price offered for the Three Kettles had been fair. But on inspection the building proved to have four fixtures and a hen which were not his to sell, and he must decline. He posted it before he could think better.

That evening he called his lodgers into the parlour: Miss Brandt, Captain Fenn, Mrs. Crumb, and young Mr. Wren. He read them the rule and put it to a vote. It passed by five to none. Marigold, under the piano, was not counted. Mrs. Crumb proposed toasted cheese, which was carried too. It was a quarter past eleven, and nobody, the landlord least of all, looked at the board.

volumes.title: The Board Comes Down
volumes.text:
Rule Twelve was never painted. A year to the day after he inherited the Three Kettles, in Emberwick, Mr. Aldous Pym took the board down and laid it on the parlour table. The house voted on his rules, one at a time.

The hours for music went first, then the rule against beans, then the one about furniture. Rent in coin was struck out to cheers. Mr. Wren painted each one out. At the end a single line was left, amended by Miss Brandt: Be in by ten, or use the scullery window quietly.

The board went back up with new words at the head. The Three Kettles. A. Pym, Landlord, and Lodgers. At ten that night Aldous stepped into the street to see whether it hung straight. It did. This time Miss Brandt, the piano tuner, was holding the front door open, and he went in by it.

volumes.title: The Bell and Bucket
volumes.text:
This Guide is compiled by Mr. Horatio Blench, late of the Excise, at the request of Mr. Tench the printer, for travellers who wish to know where a decent supper may be had within two days’ drive of Emberwick. Twelve houses are described. Each is rated in spoons, from one to five. Five spoons denote a supper without fault. The Compiler does not expect to award them.

The first house is the Bell and Bucket, in the market square at Emberwick. It is clean, plain, and loud on Thursdays. Supper was mutton and barley stew with carrots, and the heel of a loaf. The Compiler ate it alone at the corner table in eleven minutes, having a pony trap to hire.

Verdict: the stew was hot and the bread was bread. Two spoons. The trap was got from a carrier named Latchet, whose daughter is to drive it.

volumes.title: The Ploughman’s Rest
volumes.text:
Second house: the Ploughman’s Rest, at Harrow Green in the Lowlands, nine miles south of Emberwick. The Compiler, Mr. Blench, came by hired trap. The driver is Posy Latchet, aged fourteen, who talks to the pony, Turnip, and to the Compiler about equally.

The house is long and low, with one table down its whole length. At harvest every seat is taken by reapers, and the traveller sits where he is put. Supper was boiled bacon with broad beans in a parsley sauce, then a wedge of apple tart that nobody had ordered.

The bacon was tender, the sauce green and plentiful. Against this, a reaper on the Compiler’s left sang, and one on his right asked what he was writing. Verdict: three spoons, one deducted for noise. The driver ate two helpings and called it the best supper in the world. She has been to very few.

volumes.title: The Eel and Reed
volumes.text:
Third house: the Eel and Reed, on the marsh road, built on posts above water the colour of tea. The traveller from Emberwick should arrive before dusk, as the Compiler of this Guide did not. His driver, the girl Latchet, found the door by the smell of frying.

The house offers one supper, and it is eel. That night it came as a pie: eel with parsley and onion under a pale crust, and a jug of vinegar to shake over it. There were boiled potatoes. There was no alternative.

Mr. Blench has disliked eels on principle for forty years. He now finds that the principle had never tasted one. The flesh was white, mild and rich. He declines to be hurried into enthusiasm by a fish. Verdict: two spoons, and a third in pencil. The driver asked how the crust was made and was given a wink.

volumes.title: The Saltbox
volumes.text:
Fourth house: the Saltbox, at Cockle Staithe on the Grey Coast, a tarred inn so close to the tide that the cellar keeps its own hours. The Compiler, Mr. Blench, reached it in a wind that removed his hat twice. His driver, Posy Latchet, recovered it both times.

Supper was herrings, rolled in oatmeal and fried crisp, with a sharp mustard sauce and brown bread. The fish had been swimming that morning, and the landlady said so three times. They were excellent herrings. The room was full of smoke from a chimney that dislikes east winds, and the Compiler ate with his eyes shut.

Verdict: three spoons. The driver holds that a supper eaten with the eyes shut tastes better, there being nothing else to attend to. The Compiler prints this without endorsing it. She has asked whether she is in the book. She is, a little.

volumes.title: The Lantern and Net
volumes.text:
Fifth house: the Lantern and Net, at Gullsend, the last village on the Grey Coast road before it turns inland for the Fells. It rained the whole way. The Compiler arrived wet through, and his driver, Posy Latchet, wetter, having given the pony her oilskin.

The supper is called a kettle. White fish, potatoes and leeks are simmered together in milk, with butter and a good deal of pepper, and brought to table in the pot. It is eaten with a spoon and yesterday’s bread. The Compiler had three bowls and felt his boots begin to dry from the inside.

This was the best plate so far. The bedroom ceiling dripped into a basin all night, in waltz time, and the landlord sings. Verdict: four spoons, the first awarded in these pages. The driver says five, and that the Compiler is mean with spoons. He prefers the word exact.

volumes.title: The Drover’s Halt
volumes.text:
Sixth house: the Drover’s Halt, at the foot of the Northern Fells, where the cattle road from the Lowlands begins to climb. Half a mile short of it the trap shed a wheel pin. The driver, Posy Latchet, cut a new one from hazel and fitted it. The Compiler held the pony, and was told he did it well.

Supper was a suet pudding the size of a hat, of bacon and onion boiled in a cloth, with buttered cabbage. It is plain, heavy and hot, and after a wet road there is much to be said for all three.

From this entry the Guide prints two verdicts, the driver having earned an opinion. The Compiler: three spoons; a sound pudding, wanting pepper. The driver: five. The Compiler has explained that five means a supper without fault. She replies that she looked and could not find one.

volumes.title: The Cloud and Kettle
volumes.text:
Seventh house: the Cloud and Kettle, at Rooksgill, the highest inn on the Northern Fells and the halfway point of this Guide. The road up is steep. The Compiler, Mr. Blench, walked the last mile to spare the pony, on the advice of his driver, Posy Latchet, who rode.

Snow had closed the pass and the larder was low. Supper was oatcakes warm from the stone, a white crumbling cheese, heather honey, and tea strong enough to stand a spoon in. It was eaten at the one table, between two shepherds and a dog.

Afterwards the shepherds taught the party a card game called Snip the Wick. The driver won fourpence. The Compiler lost sixpence and did not mind, which he cannot account for. Verdicts. The Compiler: three spoons and a half. He does not deal in halves and will remove it before printing. The driver: five, and fourpence.

volumes.title: The Mill Tap
volumes.text:
Eighth house: the Mill Tap, at Withy Bridge on the upper Ember, a neat stone inn beside a working mill. The Compiler, Mr. Blench, sat down at seven. His driver, Posy Latchet, had taken the pony to the smith with a loose shoe and was gone until nine.

Supper was a river trout fried in butter until the skin crackled, with watercress, new bread, and half a lemon. The fish was fresh, the butter was not burnt, the cress was crisp. The room was quiet. Nobody sang.

The Compiler has looked for a fault and can name none. By his own rule that is five spoons. He finds he cannot write the figure. Verdict: four, and a blank where the reason should be. The driver had hers cold in the kitchen and says five. She asked what he had talked about at table. Nothing, he told her.

volumes.title: The Three Barges
volumes.text:
Ninth house: the Three Barges, at Lockend, where the river Ember widens and the bargemen tie up. It is a low, warm room with a bench round three sides. The Compiler, Mr. Blench, and his driver, Posy Latchet, were given the end nearest the fire.

Supper was pease pudding, thick and yellow, with slices of boiled ham and sharp pickle. It is the same every night, and the bargemen will not hear of a change.

The landlady, a Mrs. Hallam, asked to see what the Compiler was writing, and he was unwise enough to show her. She read eight entries standing up. Then she said he had rated a good many plates, and asked when he meant to begin on the suppers. He told her they were the same thing. She said he had better eat a few more. Verdicts. The Compiler: three spoons, somewhat ruffled. The driver: five.

volumes.title: The Orchard Gate
volumes.text:
Tenth house: the Orchard Gate, at Applegarth, a brick inn with pear trees along the front. The Compiler, Mr. Blench, arrived with a cold got on the river and went to bed. He records the supper on the word of his driver, Posy Latchet, who carried it up on a tray and sat on the window seat to describe it.

There was cold pork with apple sauce. Then an apple dumpling: a whole apple, cored, with a clove and sugar where the core had been, wrapped in pastry and baked, with cream.

The Compiler could taste nothing. The driver reported that the pastry was short, the apple soft but not fallen, and the cream thin. Four spoons, she said, not five. He wrote it down as given. It is the first figure in this Guide to rest on another palate, and the first time she has found a fault.

volumes.title: The Halfway Hare
volumes.text:
Eleventh house: the Halfway Hare, a roadside inn six miles south of Emberwick. The Compiler and his driver, Posy Latchet, reached it at ten, after a wrong turning that was nobody’s fault and the pony’s idea.

The larder was shut. The landlord, a Mr. Dobbs, said there was only what the family had, and sat them at the kitchen table with his wife, three children and a grandfather. Supper was bread, beef dripping, pickled onions, and tea from a brown pot that never emptied.

By the rules at the front of this Guide, that is hardly a supper. The Compiler records that the grandfather told a story about a pig and a bishop, and that he laughed until he spilt his tea, which he has not done since the Excise. Verdicts. The driver: five. The Compiler: four, and he is no longer sure what the missing spoon is for.

volumes.title: The Bell and Bucket Again
volumes.text:
Twelfth and last house: the Bell and Bucket, in the market square at Emberwick, where this Guide began. On his first visit the Compiler, Mr. Blench, gave it two spoons, having eaten alone in eleven minutes. He returned after eleven days on the road with his driver, Posy Latchet. The pony, Turnip, was stabled first, at her insistence.

Supper was mutton and barley stew, and the heel of a loaf. They sat at the same corner table for an hour and a half, arguing over every house in the book.

The stew has not changed. Verdict: five spoons, from both. The Compiler lets his first entry stand as a warning, and adds one direction for the reader: take somebody. Mr. Tench the printer wants a second book, on breakfasts. The trap is engaged, and the driver has asked for her name on the title page. It will be there.

volumes.title: Six Doors in Fog
volumes.text:
I sell spectacles. I carry them in a case with forty-eight velvet nests, and my trade is noticing what other people squint at. My name is Winifred Oake. Tonight the fog has put me down at the Turnabout, the inn at Fourways Cross, where the Coast road cuts the Fells road six miles north of Emberwick.

It is an odd house. It has a front door on each road and a staircase behind each door, and upstairs one long passage with six rooms in a row. Mrs. Tibbet, the landlady, gives me number two. “Second door along,” she says, and I count and find it.

Five other travellers are fogbound with me. A boy of eleven takes my boots to clean; he has been in the house eight days and carries them as if they might hatch. Supper is leek and potato soup. The fog leans on the windows.

volumes.title: The Wrong Boots
volumes.text:
First morning at the Turnabout, the crossroads inn where fog is keeping six of us. I am Winifred Oake, spectacle-seller, in room two. I open my door for my boots and find a pair that are not mine: black, narrow, a man’s, polished like chestnuts.

Along the passage other doors open. Mr. Lund, the notary’s clerk in room five, is holding my brown buttoned boots at arm’s length. The fiddler in three, Miss Brack, has enormous sea boots. Captain Dray in four, a retired pilot from the Grey Coast, has her small red-laced ones. Mr. Farrant the seedsman, in one, and Mrs. Vane the honey-seller, in six, have each other’s.

We meet in the middle in our stockings and trade. It is rather like a dance. Mrs. Tibbet, the landlady, apologises and blames the fog. Nothing is missing, I notice. Every boot has gone to the wrong door.

volumes.title: Chocolate for the Captain
volumes.text:
Second day of fog at the Turnabout, the inn at Fourways Cross. I am Winifred Oake. I sell spectacles, and I am watching this house, because yesterday every pair of boots came back to the wrong door.

This morning it is the trays. Captain Dray, the old sea pilot in room four, ordered shaving water. Miss Brack, the fiddler in three, ordered chocolate. I am in the passage when both doors open. She is holding a jug and a towel. He is holding a blue pot and looking into it with suspicion.

“I’ve not had this since I was a boy,” he says, and drinks it in his doorway. She tells him to keep it and hands the jug across. By noon he has ordered another pot. Mrs. Tibbet, the landlady, says the fog is getting into everyone’s head. I am not sure fog can carry a tray.

volumes.title: Supper and Suspicion
volumes.text:
There are six of us fogbound at the Turnabout, the inn where the Coast road crosses the Fells road, and by the second evening we have a mystery to go with the mutton. Things go astray upstairs. Boots first, then breakfast trays. I sell spectacles; my name is Oake; I listen.

Mr. Farrant, the seedsman, is sure Mrs. Vane, who sells marsh honey, is playing tricks. Mrs. Vane says she has better uses for her mornings. Mr. Lund, the notary’s clerk, believes someone is after his deed box and brings it to table, where it sits beside him like a seventh guest. Captain Dray thinks it a joke. Miss Brack tunes her fiddle and thinks nothing aloud.

Supper is boiled mutton with caper sauce and carrots. Mrs. Tibbet, the landlady, serves it with a red face. The new boots boy, Alfie, brings the bread, and looks at no one.

volumes.title: The Ledger and the Umbrella
volumes.text:
Third morning at the Turnabout, the fogbound inn at Fourways Cross. I am Winifred Oake, the spectacle-seller in room two, and I have begun to wake early so as not to miss anything.

Today it is things sent down and sent back. Mr. Farrant, the seedsman in room one, left his ledger to dry by the kitchen fire. Mrs. Vane, the honey-seller in six, sent her umbrella for a new rib. He opens his door on an umbrella. She opens hers on a ledger and, being a woman who cannot leave a column alone, reads it.

She walks the length of the passage and tells him that his clover seed is added up wrong on page nine, to his own loss, by four shillings. He is outraged for a minute and grateful for the rest of breakfast. They are talking at ten, about clover, and which kind suits bees.

volumes.title: A List of Pairs
volumes.text:
I am a spectacle-seller, held by fog at the Turnabout inn at Fourways Cross, and I believe in looking at a thing properly. On the third afternoon I take a card and write down everything that has gone astray.

Boots, the first morning: mine in room two changed with Mr. Lund’s in five. Miss Brack’s in three with Captain Dray’s in four. Mr. Farrant’s in one with Mrs. Vane’s in six. Trays, the second morning: three and four again. The ledger and the umbrella: one and six again.

So nothing is lost, and nothing wanders. Each room has a partner and keeps to it. A joker would vary his joke. A thief would take something. This is neither. It is a mistake, made the same way every time. I pin the card inside my case lid and feel I am looking straight at the answer without my glasses on.

volumes.title: Footsteps from the West
volumes.text:
Night at the Turnabout, the crossroads inn where six travellers have been fogbound for three days and nothing reaches the right bedroom. I am Winifred Oake, spectacle-seller, room two, and tonight I set a trap of a mild sort.

I ask Mrs. Tibbet, the landlady, to have my case of spectacles sent up to number two. I hear her repeat it in the kitchen. I go up, leave my door open a finger’s width, and sit in the dark.

Footsteps come, careful ones. They do not come from the east stair beside room one, which I climbed myself. They come from the other end, by room six, where the second staircase rises from the boot room. They pass one door and stop. A knock. Mr. Lund’s voice, in room five, says thank you. My case has gone to him. I sit and count doors on my fingers, from both ends.

volumes.title: Two and Five Make Seven
volumes.text:
Fourth morning at the Turnabout, and the fog is thinner. Before anyone is up I walk the passage in my stockings. I am Winifred Oake, and I sell spectacles. I should have looked at the doors sooner.

They have no numbers. Six brown doors. At the head of the east stair, the one from the bar, a board says Rooms One to Six, with a hand pointing. At the head of the west stair, the one from the boot room, there is only a lamp hook.

I start at the west end and count. The first door is Mrs. Vane’s, number six. The second is Mr. Lund’s, five. The third is the Captain’s. Anyone told to find the second door, who came up this way, would knock at five. Two and five. Three and four. One and six. Every pair on my card adds up to seven.

volumes.title: The Boy Who Counts
volumes.text:
The Turnabout at Fourways Cross has two staircases, and I, Winifred Oake, spectacle-seller, know that whoever carries things up the west one is counting its six doors backwards. The question is who.

Mrs. Tibbet, the landlady, and Jenny, the maid, come up from the bar by the east stair; I have watched them. The west stair rises from the boot room. One person works down there: Alfie Sedge, the boots boy, eleven years old, from a marsh farm, not a fortnight in his first place.

This evening I stand at the west stair head, apparently polishing a lens. Alfie comes up with Captain Dray’s sea boots, the Captain being in number four. His lips move. One, two, three, four. He sets them down at Miss Brack’s door, and squares the toes. He has done each task exactly as he was told. Nobody thought to tell him which end to begin.

volumes.title: What the Muddle Mended
volumes.text:
Before I say what I know, I take stock. I am Winifred Oake, spectacle-seller, four days fogbound at the Turnabout, where every boot and tray has gone to the wrong room. I have found the cause. I notice I am in no hurry.

Consider the damage. At supper Mr. Farrant the seedsman and Mrs. Vane the honey-seller agree that he will sow white clover along her dyke, and shake hands over the cheese. Captain Dray takes chocolate twice a day and is teaching Miss Brack a pilot’s song, which she plays back on the fiddle, improved.

Mr. Lund, the anxious clerk in room five, has worn a pair of my steel-rimmed samples since breakfast. He tried them when my case went to his door. He has read deeds with a headache for three years, he says, and thought it was the law. I sell him the pair at cost.

volumes.title: A Picture on Each Door
volumes.text:
I tell it in the kitchen of the Turnabout, to Mrs. Tibbet the landlady and Alfie Sedge the boots boy, with the door shut. I am Winifred Oake, the spectacle-seller from room two. I show them my card, and walk two fingers along the table from each end.

Alfie goes scarlet. He was told number four, he says, and he counted four. Mrs. Tibbet laughs until she has to hold the dresser. She has sent that child up the back stair forty times. Nobody is cross. Alfie admits, to his boots, that he is not yet steady on written numbers anyway.

So we do not paint numbers. That afternoon Captain Dray paints a picture on each door, chosen by its guest: a wheatsheaf, spectacles, a fiddle, an anchor, a quill, a bee. Alfie watches every stroke. Outside, for the first time in five days, I can see the signpost.

volumes.title: Four Roads Out
volumes.text:
The fog is gone. From the yard of the Turnabout, the inn at Fourways Cross, all four roads show clear, and six travellers are making a long business of goodbye. I am Winifred Oake, spectacle-seller, and my case is one pair lighter.

Mr. Farrant and Mrs. Vane share a cart towards the marsh, still on clover. Miss Brack takes the Coast road to a wedding, with a pilot’s song in her fiddle case. Captain Dray goes north to meet a grandchild, a tin of chocolate under his arm. Mr. Lund walks south to Emberwick, reading a deed, and does not trip.

Mrs. Tibbet says the rooms will keep their pictures. Travellers may ask for the Bee or the Anchor. This morning my boots stood outside the Spectacles, and they were mine. Alfie, the boots boy, had squared the toes. I give him sixpence and take the Fells road.
